questions.stem: The regime's reflex was always to {1} dissent rather than to {2} the discontent that produced it: grievances were pinned down by force for a decade, never met with the concessions that might have dissolved them.
questions.explanation: The colon glosses both halves: dissent is "pinned down by force" (suppress — pressure applied from above, nothing destroyed) while the underlying discontent is never soothed by concessions (mollify). Foment and placate reverse the logic in the first blank, since a regime that stirred up or appeased dissent would not be pinning it down; quash in the second blank would repeat the force idea rather than supply the contrast the sentence demands.

questions.stem: Though the garrison managed to {1} the uprising within a week, the grain tax that had provoked it remained in force, and by the following spring the countryside was in arms again.
questions.explanation: The concessive "though" requires a verb of putting down by force, and suppress and quash are the two that deliver it. Foment and incite mean the opposite — bringing the rising about — while conceal and anticipate fit the grammar and tone but describe hiding or foreseeing the revolt rather than crushing it, which would leave "in arms again" without its contrast.

questions.stem: The office of Lord High Steward is now purely {1}: it is still named in the statutes and still ceremonially filled at every coronation — hardly a post that has fallen out of use — yet it discharges none of the judicial powers that once made it the most formidable office in the realm.
questions.explanation: The sentence insists on two things at once: the office survives and is even exercised, but it does none of its former work — precisely the diagnosis vestigial makes. Obsolete, the nearest trap, claims the thing has passed out of use, which the dashed clause explicitly denies; extant and residual assert only survival or leftover quantity and say nothing about lost function.

questions.stem: The trustees' power to veto appointments, which a century ago genuinely {1} the director's ambitions, is now {2}: it is invoked at every meeting as a matter of form and has altered no decision since the war.
questions.explanation: The first blank must name what a veto once did to ambitions — held them in check (curbed) — since the second half contrasts that former force with present emptiness. Vestigial fits because the power is still fully present and regularly exercised yet accomplishes nothing; obsolete is blocked by "invoked at every meeting," which is the opposite of fallen into disuse, and nascent inverts the century-long decline the sentence describes.
